title: Energy bills and kilowatt-hours
keyIdea: Power is how fast energy is transferred: 1 watt is 1 joule every second. So energy transferred = power × time, E = P × t, with P in watts and t in seconds giving joules. A 1000 W microwave transfers 60 000 J in a minute. Joules are tiny for a home, so bills use the kilowatt-hour: the energy a 1 kW appliance transfers in 1 hour, which is 1000 W × 3600 s = 3 600 000 J. To get kWh, put the power in kilowatts and the time in hours: a 100 W TV on for 5 hours uses 0.1 × 5 = 0.5 kWh. The cost is the energy in kWh × the price per kWh. A meter counts kWh, so the energy used is the new reading minus the old one. A low-power device left on all day can cost more than a powerful one used for a few minutes.
familyTip: Find the power rating (in W or kW) on the label of a kettle, a phone charger and a TV. Guess how long each is used in a day, work out the kWh, and use the unit price on your own bill to find the daily cost.

visual.caption: How much energy does each one use? Drag each card to a box, or tap it and then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: run appliances on a joule meter, drag a power × time rectangle to make 1 kWh, convert units, rank daily costs, turn meter readings into a bill.

kid: Power tells you how fast energy is moved. One watt is one joule every second. So a 1000 W microwave moves 1000 J each second, and 60 000 J in a minute. The rule is E = P × t: energy in joules is power in watts times time in seconds.

Joules are small, so bills use a bigger unit, the kilowatt-hour (kWh). It is the energy a 1 kW device uses in 1 hour. That is 1000 W × 3600 s = 3 600 000 J. A 2 kW heater for half an hour and a 100 W lamp for 10 hours each use 1 kWh too.

To find kWh, change the power to kilowatts and the time to hours first. A 100 W TV for 5 hours is 0.1 kW × 5 h = 0.5 kWh, not 500. A 3 kW kettle for 6 minutes is 3 × 0.1 = 0.3 kWh, because 6 minutes is a tenth of an hour.

The cost is kWh × the price of one kWh. At 25p per kWh, 6 kWh costs 150p, which is £1.50. A meter counts up in kWh, so take the old reading from the new one to find what you used. A small device left on all day can cost more than a big one used for a few minutes.
adult: Ages 14 to 16. The Key Stage 3 programme of study in England lists comparing amounts of energy transferred (J, kJ, kW hour), power ratings in W and kW, and domestic fuel bills, fuel use and costs. GCSE Physics (for example AQA 8463, section 4.2.4) uses E = P t with energy in joules, power in watts and time in seconds, and asks students to compare everyday appliances by power and energy transferred.

The lab works from the definition of a watt to a real bill. Students run four appliances for 60 s on a joule meter and find the one giving 60 000 J, drag the corner of a power × time rectangle to make 1 kWh three ways along a 1 kWh curve, convert W and minutes before multiplying, rank four appliances by daily cost, and turn two meter readings into a bill. The 25p per kWh unit price is a round example, not a current tariff.

Common mistakes. Students often multiply watts by hours and call it kWh (100 W × 5 h = 500 kWh), use minutes as hours or write 6 minutes as 0.6 h, and mix seconds and hours in E = P t. Many think 1 kWh is 1000 J or 3600 J. Others assume the highest-power appliance always costs most, add or quote meter readings instead of subtracting, and write 1950p as £1950. Ask students to write the units at every step.

practice.prompt: A {=p*100} W lamp is on for {t} hours. How many kWh does it use?
practice.hint: Change watts to kilowatts (divide by 1000), then multiply by the hours.

practice.prompt: How many joules are in 1 kWh?
practice.hint: 1 kWh is 1000 W for one hour. How many seconds are in an hour?
practice.explain: 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3 600 000 J. 3600 is only the number of seconds, and 1000 J is a kilojoule.

practice.prompt: A {k} kW heater runs for {h} hours. Electricity costs 25p per kWh. What does it cost, in pence?
practice.hint: Find the kWh first (kW × hours), then multiply by the price.

practice.prompt: A 3 kW kettle boils for 6 minutes. How much energy is that in kWh?
practice.hint: 6 minutes is what fraction of an hour?
practice.explain: 6 minutes = 6 ÷ 60 = 0.1 h, so 3 kW × 0.1 h = 0.3 kWh. 18 uses minutes as hours, and 1.8 treats 6 minutes as 0.6 h.

practice.prompt: Which costs more to run each day at the same price per kWh?
choices: 20 W lights left on for 24 hours
A 3 kW kettle used for 6 minutes
practice.hint: Work out the kWh for each: kW × hours.
practice.explain: The lights use 0.02 kW × 24 h = 0.48 kWh and the kettle 3 kW × 0.1 h = 0.3 kWh, so the lights cost more even though their power is far lower.

pool.prompt: A {=p*100} W device runs for {s} seconds. How much energy does it transfer, in joules?
pool.hint: E = P × t, with P in watts and t in seconds.

pool.prompt: A 100 W TV is on for 5 hours. How much energy does it use?
pool.explain: 100 W = 0.1 kW, and 0.1 kW × 5 h = 0.5 kWh. 500 kWh multiplies watts by hours, and 20 divides instead of multiplying.

pool.prompt: A meter read {=a*100} kWh last month and {=a*100+d} kWh this month. How many kWh were used?
pool.hint: The meter only counts up. Take the old reading from the new one.

pool.prompt: A meter went from 4512 kWh to 4590 kWh. At 25p per kWh, what is the bill?
pool.hint: Find the kWh used, then multiply by 25p. Change pence to pounds at the end.
pool.explain: 4590 − 4512 = 78 kWh, and 78 × 25p = 1950p = £19.50. £1950 forgets to change pence to pounds, and £3.12 divides by the price.

pool.prompt: A 2 kW heater runs for 30 minutes. How much energy is that?
pool.explain: 2 kW × 0.5 h = 1 kWh. 60 uses minutes as hours, and 15 divides 30 by 2.

pool.prompt: Why do electricity bills use kWh instead of joules?
choices: A joule is tiny: one kWh is 3 600 000 J
A kWh is smaller and more precise
pool.hint: How many joules would a home use in a day?
pool.explain: A home uses millions of joules a day, so the kWh (3.6 million joules) gives sensible numbers. Joules measure every kind of energy, not just heat.

pool.prompt: Ali says the kettle must cost the most to run because it has the highest power. What has he forgotten?
choices: How long each appliance is on
pool.hint: Energy depends on the power and on how long it is switched on.
pool.explain: Cost depends on energy, which is power × time. A kettle is on for a few minutes a day, so a low-power device left on all day can use more kWh.

pool.prompt: A 1500 W hair dryer runs for 2 minutes. How much energy does it transfer?
pool.hint: For joules, use watts and seconds.
pool.explain: 2 minutes = 120 s, and 1500 W × 120 s = 180 000 J. 3000 J uses minutes, and 3 J uses kilowatts and minutes.
